description: Xano's platform was built with TypeScript and the latest Angular versions, with NgRx handling global state management. I wrote unit tests with Jest and contributed to internal APIs using PHP. One of our core features was a spreadsheet view of Postgres databases, so I developed frontend tools that let users craft SQL logic visually—building queries through UI controls rather than writing code directly.
As a full stack engineer at Xano, I contributed to features across the platform, from AI integrations to marketplace systems to core UI improvements.

These chat experiences also handled Node package imports and dependency management, letting users add functionality through conversation rather than manual configuration.

I designed and built two distinct marketplace systems. The Connection marketplace allowed users to discover and integrate external tools that could use Xano as their backend—expanding the platform's ecosystem beyond our native features. The Agency Partner marketplace connected users with vetted expert agencies, giving them options to get consultation or hire agencies to build solutions for them.

With my background in fine art, I was able to make design decisions independently during feature development, reducing bottlenecks and accelerating delivery. Across every feature I built, I prioritized intuitive, cohesive UX that modernized the platform while maintaining consistency with existing workflows. This meant constantly updating and refining the UI as the product evolved, ensuring new capabilities felt natural rather than tacked on.

description.content: {"link": "JobApplyPro", "url": "https://app.jobapplypro.com"} is a professional job search CRM giving users the ability to submit personalized job applications anywhere on the internet in a few clicks. Working for a small team of engineers at this stage-1 start up, I was able to develop many different areas of the front-end code base, which were built using TypeScript, React.js, and React-Redux. Based on funding, our founder ultimately decided this application would be better used as an open source tool and the start up dissolved.

picture.caption: My proposed redesign of the app's UI

description: The application is built with React and React-Redux using TypeScript. Styling was handled with CSS-in-JS Styled-Components. I was first tasked with modifying existing components to increase their flexibility and modularity. This led to me being the main engineer in charge of completing our reusable component library, with styles based on the tech lead's mockups. Aside from the component library, I built and managed our front end user authentication using role based access controls, allowing for different views based on the admin level of the user. I engineered approximately 50% of the front-end codebase, including unit testing with React-Testing-Library.

The application itself uses different layers of state management, where application state is 'held' in the Redux store and component state is dictated solely by React. This made for some interesting challenges for components that interacted with our APIs. For instance, the snack-bar component's intention is alert users as to whether an update to their information (ultimately stored in the DB) was successful. This meant that no matter where the user navigated in the application, the snack-bar needed to reach all areas of the component hierarchy while also acting independently from the Redux store as to not pollute the application state. Ultimately, I used React's Context API to create a 'useSnackBar hook' and a snack-bar alert queue that allowed any asynchronous action to be followed by a promise adding an alert to the snack-bar queue. This is just one example of the engineering problems I was privileged to explore at my time with JobApplyPro.

description: Using TypeScript, Next.js and React.js, I built a mobile friendly, responsive marketing site. This site was built to the specifications of mock ups provided by the founder.

This site allows for the dynamic display of blog posts, fetched asynchronously from mark down files hosted elsewhere. The most recent blogs are displayed as cards on the main page, displaying the blog titles on the cards and linking to new pages displaying the blogs formatted by parsing the md files. Although never launched, the idea was to have users easily share their stories and advice to the community of job seekers looking for encouragement.

{"link": "ServicesServicesServices", "url": "https://github.com/shawn-chambers/servicesServicesServices"} is a fake product page used as an example of microservice architecture. Three microservices, a product description service, an image carousel and a product reviews service can work independently but are served together in one html file through a reverse-proxy server.

description: The initial GET request from the browser goes to the proxy, retrieving the three service bundles. These bundles each individually make requests to the proxy which are forwarded to their individual Node.js servers. The node servers query their database for product data based on the product ID specified in the url. Each service independently displays the data on the browser, decoupling each service's functionality.
All data was generated programmatically using custom generation scripts and fakerjs.

The product description service shows a persisted description, feature list, and color / size options specific to each product. The names and descriptions themselves were generated programatically, all meant to sound like your favorite, "I only want this because it's 3 am and no one's here to talk me out of it" late-night, infomercial.

The purchase button is disabled until the user selects both a color and an available size. If an unavailable size is clicked, the user is told that the size is sold out. The description, features, shipping and returns, and care guide are displayed one at a time in a collapsing accordion. The chevrons turn with each selection, mimicking many popular commerce sites' functionalities.

The image carousel can be navigated with buttons, dragging the main image, or clicking a thumbnail. For the purposes of my demo app, images were hosted in AWS S3 buckets and the corresponding URLs persisted in a MongoDB.
The reviews section has an infinite scroll, fetching 10 more reviews every time the user reaches the bottom of the page.
